messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 46
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Curriculum Designer
  trauma_type: Police
  pcl5: 69

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kwame is a 46-year-old married man who works as a curriculum designer for a large urban school district. He came to therapy reluctantly, at his wife’s urging, after months of what she called “living like a soldier in a war zone.” Kwame himself would not have used that language. He would have said that he was simply paying attention, that the world required it.

The event that changed everything happened eighteen months ago, on a cool October evening. Kwame was driving home from a late meeting at the district office, taking his usual route through a residential neighborhood. He noticed a police cruiser behind him, then the flashing lights. He pulled over immediately, hands on the wheel at ten and two, exactly as he had always done. The officer approached, asked for his license and registration. Kwame complied. What happened next, he still cannot fully describe. The officer’s voice sharpened. Kwame was ordered out of the car, then onto the ground. He remembers the gravel pressing into his cheek, the weight of a knee on his back, the cold metal of handcuffs. He remembers the officer saying something about a description matching a suspect. He remembers the utter certainty, in that moment, that he might not survive this encounter. The mistake was realized after twenty minutes. The officer helped him up, apologized, said it was routine. Kwame drove home in silence. He did not tell his wife that night. He did not tell anyone.

In the weeks that followed, Kwame found himself unable to stop scanning. Driving to work, he checked his rearview mirror constantly, noting every police cruiser within sight. If one appeared behind him, his heart would slam against his ribs, his palms would sweat, and he would pull over at the next opportunity even if he had not been signaled. He began taking longer routes that avoided the neighborhood where he had been stopped. Then he started leaving the house earlier to avoid traffic altogether, reasoning that fewer cars meant fewer chances of being pulled over. His colleagues noticed he was always the first to arrive and the last to leave. He told them he was being productive. In truth, he was trying to control a world that felt increasingly dangerous.

The memories of that night did not come as a story he could tell. When his wife asked what had happened, he found himself unable to produce words that felt adequate. He would say “I was stopped by the police” and then stop, the sentence hanging unfinished, because the rest of it—the terror, the helplessness, the grinding certainty that his life could end over a mistake—felt impossible to translate into language. Sometimes, without any warning, he would be seized by the full emotional force of that night: the pressure on his back, the officer’s voice, the cold. He would be sitting at his desk reviewing a lesson plan, and suddenly his chest would tighten, his breath would come shallow, and he would have to excuse himself to the bathroom, where he would stand with his hands on the sink, waiting for the feeling to pass. There was no image with it, no clear picture in his mind—just the raw, overwhelming sense that he was in danger, that something terrible was about to happen.

His wife noticed other changes. He flinched when she touched him unexpectedly from behind. He could not sit with his back to the door in a restaurant. He stopped going to the grocery store after dark. He stopped going anywhere after dark. His social life contracted. He had always been a calm, steady presence; now he was watchful, easily startled, quick to interpret a stranger’s glance as a threat. At work, he found himself unable to concentrate on the detailed curriculum revisions that had once absorbed him. He was too busy scanning, too busy preparing for the next threat.

What finally brought him to therapy was a moment at a red light. A police cruiser pulled up beside him. Kwame’s hands began to shake. His vision narrowed. He was certain, for a few seconds, that the officer was going to get out, that he was going to be pulled from his car again. He did not move when the light turned green. The driver behind him honked. Kwame drove away, but he was trembling for the rest of the day. That night, he told his wife he needed help. He is afraid of what will happen if he does not get it—afraid that he will lose his job, his marriage, himself. But what he is most afraid of, what he cannot say out loud, is that the world he once moved through with ease is now a place of constant threat, and he does not know how to find his way back.
